newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOREIGN INVESTORS MAY ADD TO SLOVAK BANKS - FINMIN.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN INVESTORS MAY ADD TO SLOVAK BANKS - FINMIN.

text.p: Slovak Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik on the weekend said foreign investors should be allowed to participate in the privatisation of domestic banks, but not through the purchase of existing shares.
Instead, Kozlik said during a debate on official Slovak televsion, foreigners should enter the sector by adding to a bank's basic capital.
"If we allow foreign investors to enter our banks, I expect the move to be through an increase of their basic capital rather than through the sale of the existing stakes," he said.
Kozlik said foreign investors, such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), have great interest in buying stakes in Slovak banks awaiting privatisation.
Transformation of Slovakia's banking sector has been viewed by western economic organisations and EU as crucial for the further restructuring of the country's economy.

The state's holdings include a 100 percent stake in the largest savings bank, Slovenska Sporitelna a.s., and majority shares in commercial banks VUB a.s. and IRB a.s.. It also includes Slovakia's largest insurer, Slovenska Poistovna a.s., which holds about one half of the two billion crown basic capital of domestic insurers.

In January, Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar said the four of should be privatised by the end of February but the plan was delayed several times before parliament effectively postponed the privatisation until March 1997 by adding the four subjects to a list of firms excluded from privatisation.
Kozlik said bank privatisation will be carried aut after the postponement, and that an effective model for the privatisation is being sought. He did not elaborate.
"If a strong Slovak company is interested in buying into a domestic bank, it is not a catastrophe, but the company has to have a good plan and has to convince the central bank of it," Kozlik said.
"But I think large banks should be owned by more subjects, rather than allow one investor to control 50 or so percent," he added.
